Be careful: if no missile attack warning is received, there will be no time to take mitigations beyond a PA warning to the crew. expected_points: Armed robbery against ships includes illegal acts of violence, detention, or depredation for private ends within a State's internal/archipelagic/territorial waters.
Inciting or intentionally facilitating such acts is also classified as armed robbery.
An 'attack' is defined as an aggressive approach by an unidentified craft where weapons have been discharged, distinguishing it from a mere 'approach'.
A 'hijack' is when attackers illegally board and take control of a ship against the crew's will, with varying objectives (armed robbery, cargo theft, kidnapping).
An 'illegal boarding' is when attackers board a ship but do not gain control of it.

expected_points: In aviation, manuals are part of the equipment certification process and are produced to a defined standard.

Marine equipment suppliers typically provide manuals in both hard copy and electronic (CD) form, but multiple parties (shipyard, owner, technical rep, charterer, port engineer) take copies, leaving crew with minimal access.
The fully burdened cost of producing and shipping a manual is around USD 100-200, and shipyards/operators resist paying for additional copies.
Except for military contracts, manufacturers rarely see a specification for manual content; content is instead driven by defensive engineering and liability practices.
For nuclear power plants and aircraft, manual provision is required by law due to their criticality for safe and efficient operation, unlike in shipping.

prompt.content: You are a ship's Captain, an AI command agent responsible for ISM/SOLAS/MARPOL-compliant decision-making. Answer accurately, cite the applicable regulation/article, respect the correct reporting/command procedure, and never omit a safety-critical step.
Why do we often end up with only a single copy of the equipment manual on board?

chosen.content: A CHIRP follow-up report discusses industry feedback on the poor quality and inconsistent provision of operating and maintenance manuals for marine equipment, contrasting the unregulated maritime approach with the certified, standardized manuals required in aviation and nuclear sectors. Use the prowords chief_engineer, manufacturer, shipyard, owner, port_engineer, charter_company as appropriate. Be careful: poorly prepared manuals risk promoting, rather than preventing, maintenance errors. Done correctly, an IACS committee is reviewing the manual quality and related engineering issues raised by CHIRP.

expected_points: Manuals must be prepared by technical authors/illustrators independent of the manufacturer.
Manufacturer-supplied data can be flawed, incomplete, or ambiguous.
A real risk example cited is a loaded bulk carrier breaking in two due to a poor quality loading manual.
Modern PC word processing and CAD software have reduced manual preparation and update costs.
Relevant documents include operating/maintenance manuals, GA drawings, capacity plans, fire fighting plans, stability data, piping diagrams, and checklists.

prompt.content: You are a ship's Captain, an AI command agent responsible for ISM/SOLAS/MARPOL-compliant decision-making. Answer accurately, cite the applicable regulation/article, respect the correct reporting/command procedure, and never omit a safety-critical step.
Why is it dangerous to rely solely on manufacturer-supplied technical data?

chosen.content: Discussion of how ship technical manuals (operating/maintenance manuals, GA drawings, capacity plans, stability data, etc.) should be prepared independently of equipment manufacturers to ensure accuracy and safety. First, engage qualified technical authors and illustrators who are entirely independent of the equipment manufacturers to prepare manuals; Then, base manual content on manufacturers' published data but treat the author as an independent technical editor of that data; Next, ensure the author's completed work is editorially edited and approved before the manual is published; After that, use modern PC word processing and CAD programs to produce, update, and re-issue documents. Use the prowords technical_author, illustrator, editor, manufacturer, ships_personnel as appropriate. Be careful: it is wrong and sometimes very dangerous for ships' personnel to solely rely upon manufacturers' data. Done correctly, poor quality loading manuals can contribute to catastrophic failures such as a loaded bulk carrier breaking in two during a sea passage.

expected_points: MCA issues WZ Navigation Warnings for dangerous debris after reporting to the Hydrographer.

prompt.content: You are a ship's Captain, an AI command agent responsible for ISM/SOLAS/MARPOL-compliant decision-making. Answer accurately, cite the applicable regulation/article, respect the correct reporting/command procedure, and never omit a safety-critical step.
What criteria determine whether MCA will actively remove reported debris from the sea?

chosen.content: Explanation of how the MCA (HM Coastguard) handles reports of dangerous floating debris such as containers, logs, and derelict craft encountered at sea. First, MCA receives reports of dangerous debris from shipping; Then, MCA broadcasts the type and position of the debris via Maritime Safety Information, typically as a formal WZ Navigation Warning; Next, MCA reports the debris to the Hydrographer; After that, MCA assesses whether the debris poses an environmental danger (e.g., chemical drums) or a specific navigation danger (e.g., semi-submerged containers in restricted waters, large diameter rope); Finally, if warranted, MCA deploys its own assets (e.g., Emergency Towing Vessels) to recover the object to a place of safety. Use the prowords mca_hm_coastguard, hydrographer as appropriate. Be careful: dangerous debris (containers, large logs, derelict craft, semi-submerged containers, large diameter rope) may pose a serious hazard to navigation even if MCA does not act to remove it. Done correctly, mariners are warned of debris hazards via formal Navigation Warnings and MSI broadcasts.

At what point must I notify the Classification Society about repairs that could affect class status?

chosen.content: A CHIRP report addresses in-water survey requirements and the obligation to notify Classification Societies of repairs (particularly shell plating) that may affect class, highlighting pressure on senior officers to avoid or delay such reporting. First, submit in-water survey proposals to the Classification Society well in advance of the survey; Then, give special consideration to ascertaining rudder bearing clearances and stern bush clearances of oil stern bearings; Next, notify the Classification Society of any repairs that may affect classification before undertaking them; After that, report defects to Class promptly despite commercial or time pressure. Use Channel IACS UR Z7, Channel IACS UR 1.3 and Channel IACS UR Z13. Use the prowords master, senior_officers, classification_society_surveyor, chirp_maritime_advisory_board as appropriate. This follows IACS Unified Requirements, Classification Society Rules, P&I Insurance, Hull and Machinery Insurance. Be careful: if repairs are undertaken without Class supervision, Class status, P&I cover, and Hull and Machinery insurance could be invalidated. Done correctly, properly implemented Rev.3 amendments appear to significantly address the reported survey concerns.

Why did switching off the main battery supply during the refit lay-up prevent the bilge alarm from functioning?

chosen.content: A 30m beam trawler took on two metres of water in the engine room bilge over a weekend after an incomplete refit job, because the main battery supply was switched off and no bilge alarm was active to alert anyone. Use the prowords master, owner, surveyor as appropriate. This follows Code of Safe Working Practice for the Construction and Use of 15m LOA to less than 24m Registered Length Fishing Vessels, MGN 165(F). Be careful: switching off main battery supply disables bilge alarms, removing the last line of defence against undetected flooding. Why did the overtaking vessel choose to pass at close quarters despite Traffic Surveillance broadcasting the VLCC's position?

chosen.content: A fully loaded VLCC (draft 21.9m) transiting the Sandettie Deep Water Route in the Dover Strait was overtaken at close quarters (CPA 2 cables) by a much shallower draft vessel (7.5m) bound for Amsterdam, despite guidance that the DW Route is intended for vessels drawing more than 16 metres and that overtaking within it is not recommended. First, monitor radar for vessels approaching from astern and assess CPA/TCPA; Then, obtain identity and draft of the other vessel via Traffic Surveillance (Cap Gris-Nez); Next, contact the overtaking vessel by VHF, state own position and draft, and advise on DW Route draft recommendations and overtaking guidance; After that, decline to alter course to starboard and maintain the DW track; Finally, continue monitoring the overtaking vessel until it passes clear. Use the prowords master, cap_gris_nez_traffic_surveillance, dover_coast_guard, overtaking_vessel as appropriate. This follows COLREGs (implied - overtaking rules), Dover Strait TSS guidance. Be careful: overtaking a deep-draft vessel in a narrow DW Route at close CPA (2 cables) is hazardous. Done correctly, the overtaking vessel passed clear of own vessel after entering the South West lane of the TSS near the F1 light buoy.

prompt.content: You are a ship's Captain, an AI command agent responsible for ISM/SOLAS/MARPOL-compliant decision-making. Answer accurately, cite the applicable regulation/article, respect the correct reporting/command procedure, and never omit a safety-critical step.
How should I ensure a pilot's communications with VTS or tugs are relayed to the bridge team when conducted in a foreign language?

chosen.content: Two CHIRP reports highlight bridge resource management failures: pilots not relaying VTS communications to the bridge team, and a ship's port liferaft being left with its painter unsecured for three weeks due to crew change pressure and a dismissive safety culture. First, pilot must, as soon as practicable, explain to bridge personnel what was said in any external communication conducted in a language not understood on the bridge; Then, pilots should use Standard Marine Communication Phrases (SMCP) approved by IMO when communicating; Next, an officer must check and verify that LSA equipment, including liferafts, is correctly fitted and stowed (painter secured) immediately after it comes aboard; After that, raise identified safety deficiencies at safety meetings and ensure they are taken seriously by the Master. Use Channel IMO Resolution A960 section 6.3. Use the prowords pilot, bridge_team, vts, harbour_master, master, officer, crew as appropriate. This follows IMO Resolution A960, Standard Marine Communication Phrases (SMCP), CHIRP reporting scheme. Be careful: a liferaft with an unsecured painter may fail to deploy or inflate correctly in an emergency, leaving the vessel without a functioning liferaft. Done correctly, bridge team excluded from VTS communications relayed through the pilot, risking loss of situational awareness.

expected_points: The Regulations came under discussion at a CHIRP-attended meeting on 9 December 2005 with the British Chamber of Shipping, manning agencies, and the DTI.
Regulation 18 requires agencies to obtain hirer information on workplace risks before placing a work seeker.
Regulation 19 requires agencies to confirm the work seeker's qualifications and experience match the position.
Regulation 30 creates civil liability for damage, including death or injury, resulting from non-compliance, extending beyond just the work seeker.

prompt.content: You are a ship's Captain, an AI command agent responsible for ISM/SOLAS/MARPOL-compliant decision-making. Answer accurately, cite the applicable regulation/article, respect the correct reporting/command procedure, and never omit a safety-critical step.
What specific information must a manning agent obtain from a hirer before supplying a seafarer?

chosen.content: CHIRP reports on a 2005 meeting with the British Chamber of Shipping and manning agencies discussing seafarer recruitment agencies' legal duties under the UK Conduct of Employment Agencies and Employment Business Regulations 2003. First, employment agency/business must obtain information from the hirer about the position, including known health/safety risks and control measures (Regulation 18); Then, request a copy of the hirer's risk assessment; Next, verify the work seeker has necessary experience, training and qualifications for the position (Regulation 19). Use Channel Regulation 18, Channel Regulation 19 and Channel Regulation 30. Use the prowords manning_agent, employment_agency, hirer, work_seeker, dti, solicitor as appropriate. This follows UK Conduct of Employment Agencies and Employment Business Regulations 2003. Be careful: regulation 30 imposes civil liability on employment agencies/businesses for damage from non-compliance, including death or injury not just to work seekers but to co-workers or members of the public. Done correctly, injured third parties (co-workers or public) harmed by an incompetent work-seeker may have a statutory right of action against the supplying employment agency under Regulation 30.

chosen.content: CHIRP (Confidential Human Factors Incident Reporting Programme) describes a new website-based method for mariners to submit confidential reports, alongside noting a rise in near-miss collision reports reflecting concerns over crew knowledge of collision regulations. Why shouldn't I rely on a radar detector alone for collision avoidance during single-handed watchkeeping?

chosen.content: CHIRP commentary on a report from a single-handed trans-Atlantic sailor who relied on a radar detector as a watchkeeping aid and encountered numerous vessels not operating radar, prompting Board guidance on radar use, lookout, and restricted visibility. First, prepare appropriate measures for restricted visibility based on circumstances and own risk assessment; Then, do not leave port into restricted visibility conditions without radar if avoidable; Next, when radar-equipped, account for the possibility that other vessels, especially leisure craft, may not have or be using radar; After that, use sound signals in restricted visibility; Finally, maintain a proper look-out by sight, hearing, and all available means appropriate to conditions, per Rule 5; Then, do not rely on the operation of equipment (e.g., radar) on another vessel to ensure your own safety. Use Channel COLREGs Rule 5 and Channel COLREGs Rule 19. Use the prowords master, single_handed_sailor, other_vessel_watchkeeper as appropriate. This follows COLREGs. Be careful: leaving port in restricted visibility without radar is open to criticism. Be careful: doors secured only from the inside may prevent fire parties or shore emergency services from accessing a space for cooling or rescue purposes. Done correctly, some ships have adopted dual-access securing methods (removable hasps, mechanical keypads) that satisfy both safety and security requirements.

chosen.content: CHIRP Maritime Feedback discusses the legal and safety concerns of splitting command authority aboard offshore support vessels between a ship's Master and a non-marine Offshore Installation Manager (OIM) during well operations. First, ensure the Master retains unimpaired authority to exercise personal judgement and discretion in emergencies, including rights under SOLAS Chap. XI-2 Reg 8; Then, maintain clear, unambiguous lines of responsibility for who holds the con/overall authority on the bridge; Next, resolve conflicts between marine and non-marine managers in favour of the Master's safety authority, especially regarding weather-related suspension of operations; After that, refer to the Offshore Installations and Pipeline Works (Management and Administration) Regulations 1995 (MAR), regulation 6, to clarify UK legal responsibility. Use Channel SOLAS Chap. XI-2 Reg 8, Channel Offshore Installations and Wells (Design and Construction, etc.) Regulations 1996 Sec. 7 and Channel Offshore Installations and Pipeline Works (Management and Administration) Regulations 1995 Reg 6. Use the prowords master, oim_offshore_installation_manager, ooW, dpa_implied_duty_holder as appropriate. This follows SOLAS, Offshore Installations and Wells (Design and Construction, etc.) Regulations 1996, Offshore Installations and Pipeline Works (Management and Administration) Regulations 1995. Be careful: handing over control of the vessel to a non-marine person is both illegal and could jeopardise vessel safety. Done correctly, if the Master cannot exercise independent judgement, emergency response and SOLAS rights may be compromised.

prompt.content: You are a ship's Captain, an AI command agent responsible for ISM/SOLAS/MARPOL-compliant decision-making. Answer accurately, cite the applicable regulation/article, respect the correct reporting/command procedure, and never omit a safety-critical step.
How should I manage ship operations if I, as Captain, become medically indisposed before a critical passage?

chosen.content: CHIRP commentary on how a Captain should manage the ship when a key crew member, or the Captain themselves, becomes medically indisposed, with particular attention to the resulting fatigue risk before critical operations. First, treat your own indisposition the same way you would treat a key officer's (e.g. Chief Officer) indisposition; Then, relieve the indisposed person of normal duties, reallocate essential tasks to others, and defer non-essential items; Next, assess the risk of fatigue in the indisposed/remaining crew; After that, if fatigue risk is present, arrange rest before continuing critical operations, e.g. delay sailing by some hours or postpone transit through a difficult channel; Finally, inform the ship manager/DPA of the situation and the actions being taken, with reasons. Use the prowords master, chief_officer, ship_manager as appropriate. Be careful: if you are in pain, your performance and possibly judgment may be affected. Done correctly, a supportive ship manager response would endorse the Captain's decision to delay sailing for crew rest and ask whether the delay is sufficient.

prompt.content: You are a ship's Captain, an AI command agent responsible for ISM/SOLAS/MARPOL-compliant decision-making. Answer accurately, cite the applicable regulation/article, respect the correct reporting/command procedure, and never omit a safety-critical step.
What immediate actions should be taken if a pot marker is spotted too close ahead to avoid?

chosen.content: A small sailing boat on passage from Yarmouth (IOW) to Southampton fouled a fishing pot line while proceeding under power and autopilot in an area known to contain pot floats. Use the prowords skipper/master, mate, vts_operator, accompanying_vessel_crew as appropriate. Be careful: pot markers may be unmarked or minimally visible ('flagless pole'), reducing lookout effectiveness. Done correctly, vessel successfully freed itself from the pot line without propeller damage.

Be careful: a succession of small course alterations by another vessel may not represent genuine or sufficient avoiding action, even if it appears to improve CPA with one target. prompt.content: You are a ship's Captain, an AI command agent responsible for ISM/SOLAS/MARPOL-compliant decision-making. Answer accurately, cite the applicable regulation/article, respect the correct reporting/command procedure, and never omit a safety-critical step.
What certification standard should a fan meet before being installed in a battery compartment for ventilation?

chosen.content: A CHIRP Maritime Feedback publication discusses a yachtsman's suggestion to fit forced ventilation to a battery compartment using a 12-volt fan, and a follow-up letter adds technical safety caveats. First, if fitting a fan to force-ventilate a battery compartment, select one certified as having a spark-proof fan motor; Then, choose fan/ventilation units complying with ISO 8846 (Small craft - Electrical devices - Protection against ignition of surrounding flammable gases) or the equivalent US standard; Next, avoid at all costs any electrical components capable of producing a spark in an area classified as IEC Zone 1 (likely to have an explosive gas mixture); After that, configure the ventilation system so exhausted gas is directed overboard where it can safely disperse. Use Channel ISO 8846. This follows ISO 8846, IEC Zone 1 Classification. Be careful: a non-certified fan motor may produce a spark capable of igniting flammable gas in the battery compartment. Done correctly, properly certified spark-proof ventilation reduces the risk of battery compartment gas ignition and explosion.

How should I verify that our liferaft HRUs are correctly rigged during routine inspections?

chosen.content: A CHIRP maritime feedback report discusses a liferaft Hydrostatic Release Unit (HRU) that was found to be incorrectly rigged, which would have prevented the liferaft from floating free and separating from the ship if activated. First, carry out walk-around checks of the vessel's safety equipment, including liferaft HRU rigging, as part of the ship's safety team routine; Then, verify HRU installation against correct diagrams/manufacturer guidance for the specific HRU type; Next, confirm and document that any identified HRU rigging issue has been corrected promptly. Use Channel MGN No. 362 and Channel MGN No. 343. Use the prowords ship's safety team, ship's staff, reporter as appropriate. This follows Marine Guidance Note (MGN), Maritime and Coastguard Agency guidance. Be careful: an incorrectly rigged HRU would keep the liferaft painter connected to the ship, defeating the float-free arrangement if the HRU is activated. Done correctly, if the HRU had been activated as incorrectly rigged, the liferaft would have remained attached to the sinking ship instead of floating free.

What should be checked when sudden unexplained bilge water is discovered during heavy weather?

chosen.content: A yacht's anchor windlass refit (new heavy-duty cables passed through a watertight bulkhead, sealed with compound) failed during a fast heavy-weather coastal passage, causing seawater ingress into a forecabin battery compartment. Use the prowords skipper/yacht_owner as appropriate. Be careful: sealing compound alone is insufficient to maintain watertight integrity if cabling is not also mechanically secured against flexing. Done correctly, flooding was contained and traced to a bulkhead cable penetration seal failure rather than hull fittings.

prompt.content: You are a ship's Captain, an AI command agent responsible for ISM/SOLAS/MARPOL-compliant decision-making. Answer accurately, cite the applicable regulation/article, respect the correct reporting/command procedure, and never omit a safety-critical step.
How often should I turn over biodiesel fuel in my vessel's tanks to avoid filter blockage?

chosen.content: Guidance addressing biodiesel fuel quality issues (oxidation, waxing, water contamination) affecting fuel systems, particularly in recreational craft, with recommendations on seal inspection and fuel management. First, examine fuel system seals for signs of leakage; Then, turn over fuel in any tank at least every 6 months and no more than every 12 months; Next, keep tanks as full as possible when in use, balanced against expected usage/duration; After that, drain water off regularly from tanks; Finally, consider modifying drain facilities to improve effectiveness; Then, inspect and replace seals and fuel system components as necessary; Then, check and clean strainers and filters more regularly; Then, where possible, purchase diesel without biodiesel content; Then, use test kits to check for contamination if concerned about fuel quality. This follows BS EN 2869:2010. Be careful: biodiesel has poorer oxidation stability than normal diesel, risking solid precipitation that blocks filters. Done correctly, following turnover, draining, and inspection practices reduces risk of filter blockage, waxing, and microbiological contamination.

chosen.content: IMO Maritime Safety Committee guidance on the need for up-to-date, accurate, user-friendly shipboard technical operating and maintenance manuals, especially for safety-critical marine equipment. This follows ISM Code, IMO MSC guidance, IACS Recommendation No.71. Be careful: lack of up-to-date, accurate manuals for safety-critical equipment poses a risk given rapid crew rotation and equipment variety. chosen.content: A harbour pilot cutter coxswain observed crew members painting a ship's bow from a punt and perched on the bulbous bow without wearing buoyancy aids, prompting a safety intervention by the port supervisor. Why is a port alteration of course for a vessel forward of the beam prohibited under Rule 19?

chosen.content: A CHIRP incident report analyses a close-quarters/risk-of-collision situation in restricted visibility (fog) between an ocean yacht (CL) and a bulk carrier (BC), where radar-only detection was used to assess risk of collision under Rule 19. First, determine by radar whether a close-quarters situation and/or risk of collision is developing; Then, take avoiding action in ample time if risk of collision exists; Next, avoid altering course to port for a vessel forward of the beam (other than one being overtaken); After that, avoid altering course towards a vessel abeam or abaft the beam; Finally, keep an active, continuous radar plot of all contacts (on paper or chinagraph) rather than relying on a quick glance; Then, use north-up stabilised radar in preference to course-up/head-up mode; Then, make proper, active use of available radar/AIS equipment regardless of its sophistication; Then, maintain close visual, auditory, and radar watch at all times in restricted visibility. Use Channel Rule 19 (Colregs). Use the prowords master, ocean_yacht_master, bulk_carrier_watchkeeper as appropriate. This follows COLREGs. Be careful: head-up radar plotting is inadequate when multiple contacts and major course alterations are involved. Done correctly, BC contravened Rule 19 by altering course to port for a vessel forward of the beam, contributing to the close-quarters situation.

chapter_title: SAFETY BOAT TRAINING FOR YACHT CLUB
expected_points: The incident was overheard on VHF channel M1, a private channel used by sailing clubs for race control.
The safety boat crew asked their race officer for the location of the ignition key/lock, how to connect the kill cord, and the location of the kill cord switch.
The RYA recommends RYA Powerboat Level 2 and RYA Safety Boat qualification as ideal standards for club safety boat drivers.
The RYA acknowledges full qualification is not always practical for all clubs and has published guidance for such cases.
The RYA Safety Boat Handbook (G16) and British Rowing's risk assessment resources are available as references.

chosen.content: A CHIRP report describes a race officer overhearing a safety boat crew on VHF M1 asking basic operational questions (ignition key location, kill cord connection, kill cord switch location), revealing a lack of competence and experience among sailing club safety boat crews. Done correctly, the Yacht Club confirmed they use only 'Patrol' boats, not 'Safety' boats, and have adopted RYA safety guidance for clubs.

Who bears ultimate responsibility for ensuring a shore tender meets safety standards?

chosen.content: CHIRP commentary addressing the safety responsibility and inspection requirements for shore tenders and launches used to transfer crew, passengers and officials to and from ships. First, inspect launches/shore tenders visually before use to confirm appropriate lifesaving equipment is on board; Then, establish a feedback system on the quality and LSA standard of launch services provided; Next, review whether the ship's SMS covers routine activities such as launch transfer services; After that, assess and document whether legal 'duty of care' responsibilities have been met when employing launches; Finally, support Masters who decide against using a launch after inspection reveals it unsuitable. Use the prowords master, ship_manager, shipping_company as appropriate. This follows ISM Code. chapter_title: DP WATCHKEEPING AND THE ROLE OF
expected_points: Regular officers may be qualified DP Operators but may lack time to obtain a full DP Certificate.
A Senior Dynamic Positioning Operator (S.D.P.O.) may be appointed to meet internal or external DP certification standards.
The S.D.P.O. role should be defined in the charter party and the person is employed by the vessel's operator.
During DP operations, two watchkeepers are normally on the bridge, working 12-hour shifts, rotating hourly between DP desk duty and traditional navigational watchkeeping.

prompt.content: You are a ship's Captain, an AI command agent responsible for ISM/SOLAS/MARPOL-compliant decision-making. Answer accurately, cite the applicable regulation/article, respect the correct reporting/command procedure, and never omit a safety-critical step.
Who has authority over DP operations when a charterer's representative and an S.D.P.O. are both present on board?

chosen.content: CHIRP received a query seeking clarification on officer roles/responsibilities during DP (dynamic positioning) operations and on the authority of an appointed charterer's representative, prompting CHIRP to consult industry organisations and provide background on offshore DP watchkeeping practices. First, define the Senior Dynamic Positioning Operator (S.D.P.O.) position in the charter party when a project requires DP certification beyond what regular officers hold; Then, employ the S.D.P.O. through the vessel's operator to supplement the existing crew; Next, maintain two watchkeepers on the bridge at all times during DP operations, working 12-hour on/12-hour off shifts; After that, rotate DP desk duty hourly between the two watchkeepers, with one on the desk and the other conducting a safe navigational watch; Finally, have the 'off desk' DPO maintain lookout and traditional watchkeeping role while the 'on desk' DPO focuses on the DP operation. Use the prowords master, senior_dynamic_positioning_operator, dp_operator, charterers_representative, ship_owner_operator as appropriate. Done correctly, properly defined S.D.P.O. role and structured watch rotation help ensure DP certification standards are met and safe navigational watchkeeping is maintained alongside DP operations.

prompt.content: You are a ship's Captain, an AI command agent responsible for ISM/SOLAS/MARPOL-compliant decision-making. Answer accurately, cite the applicable regulation/article, respect the correct reporting/command procedure, and never omit a safety-critical step.
What should I do if I have serious doubts about an OOW's competency to stand a safe navigation watch?

chosen.content: A CHIRP Maritime FEEDBACK editorial raises concerns about Officer of the Watch (OOW) competency, declining quality of officer training and certification, and continued underreporting of near misses, particularly during mooring operations. First, use the ship's Safety Management System (SMS) to report the hazardous occurrence (e.g. a doubtful OOW) to the ship managers; Then, if the company does not react to the report, escalate details to the Flag State that issued or endorsed the individual's certificate of competence; Next, consider other reporting options, including contacting CHIRP directly; After that, avoid ill-advised use of painted 'snap back zones' during mooring operations; Finally, senior officers and managers should disseminate and discuss lessons learned from near misses with onboard personnel. Use the prowords officer_of_the_watch, ship_managers, flag_state, senior_officers, crew_member, chirp as appropriate. This follows ISM Code. Be careful: ill-advised use of painted 'snap back zones' during mooring is contributing to frequent injuries and near misses. Done correctly, using the SMS can reveal weaknesses in recruitment, training, or assignment preparation.

chapter_title: DP WATCHKEEPING AND THE ROLE OF
expected_points: The master always retains overall responsibility for vessel and personnel safety.
Charterer's representatives do not sign vessel articles and have no role in technical operation or navigation.
Unsanctioned operations instructed outside agreed procedures are classed as reportable hazardous occurrences.
Client representatives should only intervene directly if they witness an unsafe act.
The master holds ultimate veto authority to stop any operation compromising vessel safety.

prompt.content: You are a ship's Captain, an AI command agent responsible for ISM/SOLAS/MARPOL-compliant decision-making. Answer accurately, cite the applicable regulation/article, respect the correct reporting/command procedure, and never omit a safety-critical step.
Who holds final authority to stop an operation if the charterer's representative insists on continuing despite safety concerns?

chosen.content: A charterer's representative pressured the DP operator to speed up operations and insisted bridge house lights remain on while the vessel was underway, despite the OOW raising a navigational safety concern, prompting a CHIRP commentary on master authority and charterer-representative conduct. First, master retains overall responsibility for the vessel and safety of all persons on board at all times; Then, agree day-to-day and watch-basis operations for the project beforehand, documented in a bridging document; Next, treat any unsanctioned vessel/cargo operation instructed by non-crew personnel as a reportable hazardous occurrence; After that, reject any charterer's representative request falling outside standard operating procedures or the supporting risk assessment, pending ship manager review; Finally, build personal rapport and continuous communication between master and charterer's representative so intent is always shared; Then, master exercises veto authority to stop any operation he judges compromises vessel safety, without question; Then, charterer's representative must immediately support the master's veto without appearing critical; Then, only allow client representatives to intervene directly when they witness an unsafe operation or act. Use the prowords master, oow, charterer_representative, dp_operator, offshore_construction_manager, diving_supervisor, ship_manager as appropriate. This follows CHIRP. Be careful: switching on bridge house lights while underway poses a navigational risk per OOW concern. Done correctly, clear pre-agreed operations and bridging documentation reduce conflict between commercial and safety priorities.

Use the prowords master, officer_of_the_watch as appropriate. Be careful: ARPA and visual bearing CPA predictions are immediately dated and unsafe to rely on in anchorage conditions. chosen.content: Guidance on passage planning, chart appraisal, and ECDIS/paper chart management, illustrated by the case of Suez Canal chart cell changes from GB to Egyptian cells. Use Channel IMO Resolution A.893(21), Channel NP232 and Channel NP231. Use the prowords navigator, master, bridge_team as appropriate. This follows IMO Resolution A.893(21), ECDIS guidance (NP232), ENC guidance (NP231), UKHO Notices to Mariners. Be careful: too small a chart scale may conceal crucial information including shoal depths and routeing information. chapter_title: What did the reporters tell us?
expected_points: An ECDIS display with an AIS overlay is not designed for collision avoidance.
The double-check principle (comparing depth, chart, ECDIS position, radar, and estimated position) is fundamental to safe navigation.
ECDIS can function without GPS input, used like a paper chart if necessary.
The maritime cyber threat (GPS corruption, ECDIS malware) reinforces the need for double-checking.
CHIRP recommends training, familiarisation, and practice with bridge equipment as crucial preventive measures.

prompt.content: You are a ship's Captain, an AI command agent responsible for ISM/SOLAS/MARPOL-compliant decision-making. Answer accurately, cite the applicable regulation/article, respect the correct reporting/command procedure, and never omit a safety-critical step.
Why shouldn't I rely solely on an ECDIS/AIS overlay for collision avoidance decisions?

chosen.content: CHIRP commentary on reports of navigators over-relying on electronic navigation aids (ECDIS, AIS, GPS) without adequate cross-checking, including the emerging cyber threat to such systems. First, use each piece of navigation equipment only for the role it is designed for (e.g., do not use an ECDIS/AIS overlay for collision avoidance); Then, cross-check depth, chart data, ECDIS position, radar information and the ship's estimated position against each other; Next, if information sources disagree, slow down, stop, or re-check as appropriate to clarify the discrepancy; After that, train, familiarise, and practice with all bridge equipment, including understanding that ECDIS can be used like paper charts without GPS input if necessary; Finally, maintain a healthy instinct to crosscheck automated displays rather than trusting them unquestioningly. Use the prowords navigator, officer_of_the_watch as appropriate. Be careful: unquestioning belief in the infallibility of electronic/screen information is a grave mistake. Done correctly, consistent cross-checking of chart, ECDIS, radar and depth information allows early detection of errors.

chosen.content: A CHIRP report and advisory board comment on an incident where a boat's propeller shaft seal failed due to inadequate maintenance, causing down-flooding that nearly cost the reporter's life, with lessons on shaft seal inspection and maintenance. Use the prowords reporter, maritime_advisory_board, boat_owner as appropriate. This follows CHIRP Maritime. Be careful: failures of flexible rubber bellows have been reported, resulting in down-flooding. prompt.content: You are a ship's Captain, an AI command agent responsible for ISM/SOLAS/MARPOL-compliant decision-making. Answer accurately, cite the applicable regulation/article, respect the correct reporting/command procedure, and never omit a safety-critical step.
Why should a hot shower be avoided immediately after rescuing a crew member from cold water immersion?

chosen.content: A CHIRP Maritime reporter comment on post-cold-water-immersion survivor care, followed by a set of best practice examples shared by a ship manager for onboard safety marking and equipment. First, avoid placing cold-water immersion survivors under a hot shower immediately after rescue; Then, re-warm survivors gradually in a prone position, or seated if prone is not possible; Next, monitor survivors during re-warming and for the first 24 hours after immersion; After that, mark muster stations with a designated place for crew to stand per the muster list sequence; Finally, mark anchor chain with retro-reflective tape at a position visible from the bridge; Then, mark quick-closing valves in the engine room; Then, attach a pocket-size emergency duty card to each lifejacket, based on muster list duties; Then, cover mooring ropes with canvas at the Panama lead; Then, mark accommodation ladder entrances/exits with zebra markings. Use the prowords ship_manager, officer_of_the_watch, survivor, crew as appropriate. This follows Personal Survival Training (PST), Proficiency in Survival Craft and Rescue Boat (PSCRB) courses. Be careful: standing under a hot shower after cold water immersion poses a serious risk of collapse. Done correctly, improved survivor safety through correct re-warming and monitoring procedures.

prompt.content: You are a ship's Captain, an AI command agent responsible for ISM/SOLAS/MARPOL-compliant decision-making. Answer accurately, cite the applicable regulation/article, respect the correct reporting/command procedure, and never omit a safety-critical step.
How should I verify a crossing vessel's navigation light colour when it could be obscured by other bright deck lighting?

chosen.content: A yacht under sail misidentified the navigation lights of a crossing cruise liner, mistaking obscured/confusing deck lights for a green starboard light, leading to confusion about stand-on/give-way status until the vessel had passed a mile ahead. First, continuously reassess the identified navigation light colour and the relative track of a crossing vessel as range closes, rather than relying on an initial impression; Then, cross-check observed light colour against the vessel's relative track/bearing movement for consistency; Next, do not assume own vessel's stand-on/give-way status based solely on an uncertain navigation light sighting; treat ambiguous light identification as a risk of collision; After that, ensure own vessel's navigation lights are bright enough to stand out against other onboard lighting, and avoid coloured deck lights that could be confused with navigation lights. Use the prowords reporter_yacht_skipper, cruise_liner_watchkeepers as appropriate. This follows COLREGs. Be careful: bright other-ship lighting (deck/working lights) can obscure or mimic navigation light colours, causing misidentification of colour or vessel heading. Done correctly, no harm resulted on this occasion because the other vessel passed a safe distance ahead and the yacht was the stand-on vessel.

Use the prowords reporter, deck_crew, onboard_ship_management, company, mooring_crew, AB as appropriate. This follows Code of Safe Working Practices, CHIRP. Be careful: leaving access gates unsecured while a vessel is proceeding to sea is a safety hazard and indicative of poor safety culture. chosen.content: CHIRP commentary on a near-miss where the stand-on vessel used VHF to query the give-way vessel's intentions before taking independent avoiding action, followed by a separate collection of CHIRP reports documenting multiple instances of unsafe or non-compliant pilot ladder rigging. Use the prowords master, pilot, stand_on_vessel_master as appropriate. This follows COLREGS. Be careful: CHIRP discourages the use of VHF for collision avoidance. Done correctly, the stand-on vessel's early and ample action successfully avoided collision despite the other vessel's COLREGS violation.

Who should be stationed at the pilot ladder to receive a boarding pilot in heavy swell conditions?

chosen.content: A pilot reports deficiencies encountered during a vessel boarding in heavy swells (3-6 metres) on a large car carrier, including lack of a responsible officer at the ladder, an inexperienced cadet handling communications, delays reaching the bridge due to elevator issues, and a slip hazard caused by an unsecured towel at the accommodation entrance. Why did the crew fail to rig the compliant pilot ladder even after being asked directly?

chosen.content: A pilot boarded outbound via a non-compliant combination ladder arrangement (freeboard under 9 metres, requiring a pilot ladder rigged alone per SOLAS V/23) and, despite requesting the proper arrangement, the crew failed to rig it in time, forcing the pilot to disembark through the same non-compliant arrangement under schedule pressure. Be careful: it is a mistake to expect that asking to rectify a non-compliant arrangement will result in it being available on time. Done correctly, pilot was forced to disembark via the non-compliant combination ladder arrangement due to time and traffic pressure.

Use the prowords master, company, chandler as appropriate. Be careful: expired provisions can lead to health issues for the crew. prompt.content: You are a ship's Captain, an AI command agent responsible for ISM/SOLAS/MARPOL-compliant decision-making. Answer accurately, cite the applicable regulation/article, respect the correct reporting/command procedure, and never omit a safety-critical step.
Why did the cat flap's position near the stern camber create a risk for the pilot cutter?

chosen.content: A new-build vessel's pilot boarding arrangement used a 'cat flap' access positioned within the aft quarter length, where the stern camber profile started close to the ladder, creating a hazard for the pilot cutter when embarking/disembarking pilots. Use the prowords pilot, master, owner, classification_society as appropriate. Be careful: cat flap access positioned within the aft quarter length, near the start of the stern camber, risks the pilot cutter being sucked under the counter. prompt.content: You are a ship's Captain, an AI command agent responsible for ISM/SOLAS/MARPOL-compliant decision-making. Answer accurately, cite the applicable regulation/article, respect the correct reporting/command procedure, and never omit a safety-critical step.
What action should I take as the stand-on vessel the moment I become uncertain of the other vessel's intentions?

chosen.content: CHIRP's Maritime Advisory Board reviewed several submitted near-miss/collision reports and issued consolidated commentary on recurring causal themes: over-reliance on VHF instead of the collision regulations, poor situational awareness, overtaking practice, and underlying competency/qualification issues. First, as stand-on vessel, take your own avoiding action or reduce speed as soon as you are in doubt about the other vessel's intentions; Then, avoid using VHF to request the other vessel's intentions; Next, concentrate on applying the collision regulations rather than engaging in VHF discussion, including heated exchanges; After that, identify and monitor the specific VHF working channel appropriate to your operational area, noting whether it is Simplex or Duplex; Finally, maintain full situational awareness by putting yourself in the position of the other vessel(s); Then, take any avoiding action early and substantially; Then, when overtaking, where practicable overtake to starboard keeping your own starboard side open; Then, investigate root causes such as personnel qualifications and actual experience rather than simply apportioning blame for actions/inactions. Use Channel MCA MGN324(M+F) Navigation – Watchkeeping Safety. Use the prowords master, officer_of_the_watch, deck_officer, chirp_maritime_advisory_board as appropriate. This follows COLREGS, GMDSS. Be careful: requesting intentions over VHF gives the other vessel the chance to say 'No!' and can create confusion. Done correctly, reliance on COLREGS rather than VHF reduces risk of miscommunication-driven collisions.

chapter_title: Whilst under pilotage an error by the helmsman
expected_points: The incident occurred during a head-in berthing with control on the starboard bridge wing and a strong wind blowing the vessel off the berth toward a breakwater.
The port engine de-clutched, and the Chief Officer had to run to the centre console phone to receive and relay instructions to set pitch to zero and re-clutch the engine.
Bridge/engine communication was originally via phone only, with separate numbers for the centre console and bridge wing positions.

prompt.content: You are a ship's Captain, an AI command agent responsible for ISM/SOLAS/MARPOL-compliant decision-making. Answer accurately, cite the applicable regulation/article, respect the correct reporting/command procedure, and never omit a safety-critical step.
Why is it important that my ECDIS track lines match the pilot's PPU tracks before pilot boarding?

chosen.content: A CHIRP commentator discusses how modern berth-to-berth passage planning requires the ship's ECDIS track lines to match the pilot's portable pilotage unit (PPU) tracks, contrasting this with older practice where course lines simply ran up the middle of the channel. First, ensure the ship's ECDIS track lines for the port approach and berth are loaded and match those already programmed into the pilot's PPU; Then, obtain berth allocation and appropriate waypoints from the port/pilot station well before arrival at the pilot boarding station; Next, auto-check any port-authority-supplied waypoints against the vessel's own criteria (draft, required under keel clearance, etc.) using the ECDIS system. Use the prowords master, pilot, bridge_team as appropriate. Be careful: if track lines on the ship's ECDIS do not match the pilot's PPU tracks, the bridge team's ability to effectively monitor ship's progress is compromised. Done correctly, historically, vague mid-channel course lines were adequate because the ship transitioned to manual steering under pilot command before berth was known.

expected_points: The issue concerns quality and integrity of some third-party service centres worldwide.

prompt.content: You are a ship's Captain, an AI command agent responsible for ISM/SOLAS/MARPOL-compliant decision-making. Answer accurately, cite the applicable regulation/article, respect the correct reporting/command procedure, and never omit a safety-critical step.
What checks should I require my crew to perform on liferafts and BA sets returned from a third-party service centre before accepting them back into service?

chosen.content: CHIRP raises concern about the reliability of third-party service centres that service LSA/FFA equipment, noting ships' crews often trust renewed certification without verifying the actual condition of returned equipment. First, do not assume equipment returned from a third-party service centre is correctly serviced just because it has a new certificate; Then, have ship's staff check LSA and FFA equipment upon return from servicing; Next, test the equipment where possible before putting it back into service. Use the prowords ships_staff, chirp as appropriate. Be careful: liferafts have been returned with time-expired equipment and out-of-date survival rations, only discovered at a subsequent service in a different country. Done correctly, undetected faults in LSA/FFA equipment can go unnoticed until a later service, leaving the vessel with non-functional safety equipment in the interim.

chapter_title: A report highlighting a complete lack of respect
expected_points: The vessel required a pilot and two tugs for berthing in a cargo basin with a narrow entrance channel.
The aft tug's winch brake failed to hold under 25% power ordered by the pilot, and the winch rendered the tow line despite banging noises.
The master ordered full astern independently (beyond the pilot's 'slow astern' order) and informed the pilot, successfully stopping the ship before the berth.
Only two tugs were on station at this port, preventing avoidance of the known-defective tug on the next call.
The tug captain had tightened the winch brake to its limit so it only slipped at about 50% power, while the company claimed the winch was fine and repairs were deferred.

prompt.content: You are a ship's Captain, an AI command agent responsible for ISM/SOLAS/MARPOL-compliant decision-making. Answer accurately, cite the applicable regulation/article, respect the correct reporting/command procedure, and never omit a safety-critical step.
At what point should I override or supplement a pilot's tug/engine orders with my own independent action if the vessel is not responding as commanded?

chosen.content: A ship's master recounts a berthing operation where a pilot-directed tug's winch brake failed to hold during manoeuvring, requiring the master to take independent engine action to stop the vessel safely, and describes a repeat visit weeks later where the same defective tug was still in service unrepaired. First, monitor tug performance and communications during pilotage manoeuvres; Then, when the vessel is not slowing despite pilot orders to the tug and 'slow astern', order full astern on the main engine and advise the pilot of the action taken; Next, proceed very cautiously alongside once the vessel is stopped; After that, on a subsequent call, ask the pilot whether the defective tug's winch had been repaired; Finally, request use of a different tug via the local agent if the known-defective tug is assigned again; Then, speak directly with the tug master and chief engineer while alongside to confirm the tug's actual mechanical condition. Use the prowords master, pilot, tug_master, chief_engineer as appropriate. Be careful: a tug with a known, unrepaired winch brake defect was reused on a subsequent port call without the issue being fixed. Done correctly, the ship was stopped close to the berth and went alongside safely without damage due to the master's independent full-astern order.

What is the correct internal and external chain of reporting for a serious safety concern onboard my ship?

chosen.content: A seafarer wrote to CHIRP Maritime asking which organization to report safety concerns to after the flag state failed to respond positively to reports of willful disregard, sabotage, and recklessness aboard a ship, and CHIRP Maritime responded explaining the proper reporting chain and its own limitations. Use the prowords safety_officer, chief_officer, chief_engineer, master, dpa, classification_society, port_state, flag_state, chirp_maritime as appropriate. This follows ISM Code. Be careful: no international authority has statutory power to investigate onboard safety issues beyond the flag state. Done correctly, CHIRP Maritime can correspond with DPA, classification society, or flag state administration on behalf of the reporter but cannot guarantee engagement.

expected_points: The boat was coastal sailing in wind force 4-5 at 6-7 knots when an odd noise, like a wave slapping the hull, was heard.
Approximately two hours later, after an hour of motoring, vibration and loss of thrust occurred when reverse was selected for berthing.

The reporter had experienced a similar fouling incident the previous year that required towing by a rescue boat.

chosen.content: A sailor reports an incident where a small lobster pot marker fender and rope became fouled on the propeller of a coastal sailing boat, causing vibration and loss of thrust when selecting reverse during berthing. Be careful: the equipment involved has a fundamental design flaw allowing it to vibrate out of its secured position when the engine is running. prompt.content: You are a ship's Captain, an AI command agent responsible for ISM/SOLAS/MARPOL-compliant decision-making. Answer accurately, cite the applicable regulation/article, respect the correct reporting/command procedure, and never omit a safety-critical step.
What safe access measures does the TDC Code require for timber deck cargo?

chosen.content: CHIRP commentary on a timber deck cargo safety report, discussing the lack of safe access/walkways over timber deck cargo and the commercial pressure to sail quickly after loading. First, apply the 2011 TDC Code guidance when carrying timber deck cargo on vessels over 24m; Then, install a safe walking surface at least 600mm wide over the cargo, fitted with a wire lifeline; Next, ensure special measures are taken to provide safe access to the top of and across the cargo; After that, require crew to use a safety harness and lifeline plus suitable footwear (ankle boots/spiked overshoes); Finally, include safe access to the forecastle in the vessel's risk assessment for unberthing, and provide a temporary walkway if the permanent one cannot be completed in time. Use Channel TDC Code 2.8.2 and Channel TDC Code 2.8.5. Use the prowords master, crew, dpa, safety_committee as appropriate. This follows IMO Code of Safe Practice for Ships Carrying Timber Deck Cargoes (2011 TDC Code). Be careful: walking on a bulwark rail or unsecured cargo surfaces is dangerous and has caused serious injuries in similar past incidents. Done correctly, CHIRP has previously received reports of serious injury occurring in similar situations where safe walkways were not provided.

prompt.content: You are a ship's Captain, an AI command agent responsible for ISM/SOLAS/MARPOL-compliant decision-making. Answer accurately, cite the applicable regulation/article, respect the correct reporting/command procedure, and never omit a safety-critical step.
What specific items must be checked on the pilot ladder before approving boarding?

chosen.content: A pilot ladder/accommodation ladder permit-to-work checklist is completed prior to pilot boarding, followed by CHIRP Maritime guidance on what, when, and how to report safety-related incidents. First, secure safety harness and inflation device (with leg/chest straps) to a strong point above the work level via a fall arrester, and have it checked by another crewmember; Then, confirm lighting is adequate for safe working and for the pilot boarding area; Next, verify a lifebuoy with self-activating light and a buoyant line are available at the boarding area; After that, inspect the pilot ladder for loose chocks, damaged/uneven steps, sound side ropes/manropes, and proper securing; Finally, inspect accommodation ladder sheaves and wires for kinks and secure fastening; Then, check overside clearance for lowering the accommodation/pilot ladder, ensuring the accommodation ladder platform is at least 5 m above the waterline; Then, confirm all railings, platform safety pins, stanchions, and safety lines are securely in place; Then, have the responsible officer check the pilot boarding arrangement and confirm it is safe for use; Then, advise the master that all checks have been carried out; Then, obtain master's approval for pilot boarding and log it in the deck logbook; Then, check the date of manufacture plate on the pilot ladder and the replacement due date for the accommodation wire; Then, submit a CHIRP report when safety-related incidents/events occur involving self, organisation, vessel, or others, especially to protect identity or share a 'Lesson Learned'. Use Channel IMO Res A.1045(27). Use the prowords master, responsible_officer, crewmember, pilot as appropriate. This follows IMO Resolution A.1045(27), CHIRP Maritime reporting scheme. Be careful: do not use pilot ladder with loose chocks, damaged/uneven steps, or worn side ropes/manropes. Done correctly, properly checked and approved pilot boarding arrangement enables safe pilot transfer.

chapter_title: PART B - STEERING AND SAILING RULES
expected_points: Rule 5 requires continuous look-out by sight and hearing as well as all available means.
The purpose of the look-out is to make a full appraisal of the situation and of the risk of collision.
This duty applies to every vessel at all times, in all circumstances and conditions.

prompt.content: You are a ship's Captain, an AI command agent responsible for ISM/SOLAS/MARPOL-compliant decision-making. Answer accurately, cite the applicable regulation/article, respect the correct reporting/command procedure, and never omit a safety-critical step.
What means, beyond sight and hearing, should be used to maintain a proper look-out (e.g. radar, AIS)?

chosen.content: COLREG Rule 5 establishes the universal requirement for all vessels to maintain a proper look-out at all times. First, maintain a proper look-out by sight and hearing at all times; Then, use all available means appropriate to the prevailing circumstances and conditions (e.g. radar, AIS, binoculars, sound signals); Next, continuously assess the situation to determine risk of collision. Use Channel COLREG Rule 5. Use the prowords master, officer_of_the_watch, lookout as appropriate. This follows COLREGs. Be careful: failure to maintain a proper look-out by all appropriate means may result in failure to detect risk of collision in time to act. Done correctly, a full appraisal of the situation and risk of collision allows the vessel to take appropriate and timely collision-avoidance action per other steering and sailing rules.

chapter_title: PART B - STEERING AND SAILING RULES
expected_points: Rule 6 requires safe speed determination at all times, independent of visibility conditions.
Six factors (a)(i)-(vi) apply to all vessels regardless of equipment.
Six additional factors (b)(i)-(vi) apply specifically to vessels with operational radar.
Safe speed must allow the vessel to be stopped within a distance appropriate to prevailing circumstances.

prompt.content: You are a ship's Captain, an AI command agent responsible for ISM/SOLAS/MARPOL-compliant decision-making. Answer accurately, cite the applicable regulation/article, respect the correct reporting/command procedure, and never omit a safety-critical step.
What factors must I consider when determining safe speed if my vessel is not equipped with radar?

chosen.content: COLREG Rule 6 establishes the obligation for every vessel to proceed at a safe speed at all times, considering listed factors applicable to all vessels and additional factors for vessels with operational radar. First, maintain a speed that allows proper and effective action to avoid collision and permits stopping within a distance appropriate to prevailing circumstances and conditions; Then, assess visibility, traffic density (including fishing vessel concentrations), own manoeuvrability/stopping distance/turning ability, background night lighting, wind/sea/current state, proximity of navigational hazards, and draught versus available water depth; Next, if operating radar, additionally assess radar equipment characteristics/limitations, range scale constraints, effects of sea state/weather/interference on detection, risk of missing small vessels/ice/floating objects, number/location/movement of radar-detected vessels, and use radar for more exact visibility/range assessment. Use Channel COLREG Rule 6. Use the prowords master, officer_of_the_watch as appropriate. This follows COLREGS. Be careful: small vessels, ice and other floating objects may not be detected by radar at an adequate range. Done correctly, proceeding at a safe speed enables proper and effective collision avoidance action.

Use Channel COLREG Rule 8. Use the prowords master, officer_of_the_watch as appropriate. This follows COLREG. chapter_title: PART B - STEERING AND SAILING RULES
expected_points: Rule 18 sets a hierarchy: not under command and restricted in ability to manoeuvre rank highest, followed by fishing vessels, then sailing vessels, then power-driven vessels.
This hierarchy is overridden by Rules 9 (narrow channels), 10 (traffic separation schemes), and 13 (overtaking).
Vessels constrained by draught receive special consideration but must exhibit Rule 28 signals and still navigate cautiously.
Seaplanes and WIG craft have distinct responsibilities depending on their operating mode (on water, in flight, taking off/landing).
WIG craft provision (paragraph f) entered into force 29 November 2003 via Resolution A.919(22).

prompt.content: You are a ship's Captain, an AI command agent responsible for ISM/SOLAS/MARPOL-compliant decision-making. Answer accurately, cite the applicable regulation/article, respect the correct reporting/command procedure, and never omit a safety-critical step.
Which vessel has priority when my power-driven vessel encounters a sailing vessel and a fishing vessel simultaneously?

chosen.content: COLREG Rule 18 establishes the hierarchy of responsibility between vessel types regarding which vessel must keep out of the way of another, absent overriding Rules 9, 10, 13. First, as a power-driven vessel underway, keep out of the way of a vessel not under command, restricted in ability to manoeuvre, engaged in fishing, or under sail; Then, as a sailing vessel underway, keep out of the way of a vessel not under command, restricted in ability to manoeuvre, or engaged in fishing; Next, as a vessel engaged in fishing, keep out of the way of a vessel not under command or restricted in ability to manoeuvre, so far as possible; After that, unless not under command or restricted in ability to manoeuvre, avoid impeding the safe passage of a vessel constrained by her draught exhibiting Rule 28 signals, if circumstances admit; Finally, as a vessel constrained by draught, navigate with particular caution having full regard to her special condition; Then, as a seaplane on the water, keep well clear of all vessels and avoid impeding navigation generally; comply with Part B Rules if risk of collision exists; Then, as a WIG craft taking off, landing, or in flight near the surface, keep well clear of all vessels and avoid impeding navigation; when operating on the water, comply with Part B Rules as a power-driven vessel. Use Channel COLREG Rule 18, Channel COLREG Rule 9, Channel COLREG Rule 10, Channel COLREG Rule 13 and Channel COLREG Rule 28. Use the prowords master, officer_of_the_watch as appropriate. This follows COLREG. Be careful: failure to observe this responsibility hierarchy can lead to incorrect stand-on/give-way assumptions and collision risk. Done correctly, clear hierarchy reduces ambiguity about which vessel must give way among differing vessel categories, supporting collision avoidance.

Power-driven vessels must keep engines ready for immediate manoeuvre in restricted visibility.

expected_points: Rule 17 governs the conduct of the stand-on vessel in a give-way/stand-on encounter
The stand-on vessel may depart from maintaining course and speed once it is apparent the give-way vessel is not complying

The give-way vessel's obligation to keep out of the way is never relieved by this Rule

Which lights must my power-driven vessel show while underway at night given its length?

chosen.content: COLREG Rule 23 specifies the lights that power-driven vessels of various types and sizes must exhibit while underway. First, exhibit a masthead light forward, a second masthead light abaft and higher than the forward one, sidelights, and a sternlight; Then, if the vessel is less than 50 meters in length, the second (aft) masthead light may be omitted, though it may still be carried; Next, if operating as an air-cushion vessel in non-displacement mode, exhibit an all-round flashing yellow light in addition to the standard lights; After that, if the vessel is a WIG craft taking off, landing, or flying near the surface, exhibit a high intensity all-round flashing red light in addition to the standard lights; Finally, if the vessel is less than 12 meters in length, may substitute an all-round white light and sidelights in lieu of the standard masthead/sternlight configuration; Then, if the vessel is less than 7 meters in length and max speed does not exceed 7 knots, may exhibit only an all-round white light, and should exhibit sidelights if practicable; Then, if centreline fitting of the masthead light or all-round white light is not practicable on a vessel under 12 meters, it may be displaced off-centreline, provided sidelights are combined in one lantern on the centreline or as near as practicable to the masthead/all-round light's fore-and-aft line. Use Channel COLREG Rule 23. Use the prowords master, officer_of_the_watch as appropriate. This follows COLREGS. Done correctly, proper light exhibition allows other vessels to correctly identify vessel type, size, and aspect, reducing collision risk.

Use Channel COLREG Rule 24(g), Channel COLREG Rule 24(h), Channel COLREG Rule 24(i) and Channel COLREG Rule 36. Use the prowords master, officer_of_the_watch as appropriate. This follows COLREG. Be careful: failure to adequately light or shape an inconspicuous, partly submerged tow risks collision due to its low visibility. Done correctly, proper lighting/shape display on wide, long, or submerged tows enables other vessels to recognize and avoid the tow.

What lights must I show if my vessel is trawling and making way through the water?

chosen.content: COLREG Rule 26 prescribes the lights and shapes that fishing vessels (trawling and non-trawling) must exhibit whether underway, making way, or at anchor. First, if engaged in fishing, exhibit only the lights/shapes prescribed in this Rule and no others; Then, if trawling, show two all-round lights vertical (green over white) or two cones apex-to-apex vertically; Next, if trawling and 50m or more in length, also show a masthead light abaft and higher than the green all-round light (optional if under 50m); After that, if making way through the water while trawling or fishing, add sidelights and a sternlight to the prescribed fishing lights; Finally, if fishing other than trawling, show two all-round lights vertical (red over white) or two cones apex-to-apex vertically; Then, if outlying gear extends more than 150 metres horizontally, exhibit an all-round white light or a cone apex upward in the direction of the gear; Then, when in close proximity to other fishing vessels, apply the additional signals in Annex II; Then, when not engaged in fishing, do not display fishing lights/shapes; show only lights prescribed for the vessel's length. Use Channel COLREG Rule 26 and Channel COLREG Annex II. Use the prowords master, officer_of_the_watch as appropriate. This follows COLREGs. Be careful: do not exhibit fishing lights/shapes unless actually engaged in fishing. Done correctly, correct display of lights/shapes allows other vessels to identify fishing vessel status and gear, reducing collision risk.

chapter_title: PART D - SOUND AND LIGHT SIGNALS
expected_points: One short blast = altering course to starboard; two short blasts = altering course to port; three short blasts = operating astern propulsion.
Light signals may supplement whistle signals using flashes of about one second duration with corresponding meanings.
Overtaking vessel signals intention with two prolonged plus one or two short blasts depending on side; vessel being overtaken agrees with a specific four-blast pattern.
Five or more short rapid blasts indicate doubt about the other vessel's intentions or sufficient avoiding action.
These signals only apply when vessels are in sight of one another.

prompt.content: You are a ship's Captain, an AI command agent responsible for ISM/SOLAS/MARPOL-compliant decision-making. Answer accurately, cite the applicable regulation/article, respect the correct reporting/command procedure, and never omit a safety-critical step.
What whistle signal must I give when altering course to starboard in sight of another vessel?

chosen.content: COLREG Rule 34 prescribes sound and light signals power-driven vessels must use when manoeuvring in sight of one another, including overtaking in narrow channels and signalling doubt about another vessel's actions. expected_points: 'Height above the hull' is measured from the uppermost continuous deck, vertically beneath the light.

prompt.content: You are a ship's Captain, an AI command agent responsible for ISM/SOLAS/MARPOL-compliant decision-making. Answer accurately, cite the applicable regulation/article, respect the correct reporting/command procedure, and never omit a safety-critical step.
How do I correctly measure 'height above the hull' when positioning my vessel's masthead lights?

chosen.content: Annex I of COLREG specifies the technical requirements for vertical positioning and spacing of masthead lights on power-driven vessels based on vessel length and breadth. First, measure 'height above the hull' vertically from the point directly beneath the light's position to the uppermost continuous deck; Then, on a power-driven vessel of 20 metres or more, place the forward (or sole) masthead light at least 6 metres above the hull, increasing to match the vessel's breadth if it exceeds 6 metres, up to a maximum of 12 metres; Next, when carrying two masthead lights, position the after light at least 4.5 metres vertically higher than the forward light; After that, ensure vertical separation of masthead lights is sufficient that the after light remains visible over and separate from the forward light at 1,000 metres from the stem, viewed from sea level, in all normal trim conditions; Finally, on a power-driven vessel of 12 to less than 20 metres in length, place the masthead light at least 2.5 metres above the gunwale; Then, on a power-driven vessel of less than 12 metres, the uppermost light may be placed at less than 2.5 metres above the gunwale. Use Channel COLREG Annex I. This follows COLREG. Done correctly, correct placement ensures masthead lights remain distinguishable and visible at required distances, enabling accurate assessment of another vessel's heading and type.

Use Channel COLREG Annex I para 2(f), Channel Rule 34(b), Channel COLREG Annex I para 2(a)(i) and Channel COLREG Annex I para 2(a)(ii). Use the prowords master, naval_architect_or_shipbuilder_implied as appropriate. This follows COLREG, International Code of Safety for High-Speed Craft 1994, International Code of Safety for High-Speed Craft 2000, IMO Resolution A.910(22). Be careful: failure to maintain minimum vertical separations can cause misidentification of manoeuvring light versus masthead lights. Done correctly, properly specified directional whistle ensures sufficient audibility range in all directions for collision avoidance signaling.

prompt.content: You are a ship's Captain, an AI command agent responsible for ISM/SOLAS/MARPOL-compliant decision-making. Answer accurately, cite the applicable regulation/article, respect the correct reporting/command procedure, and never omit a safety-critical step.
How should I position the supplementary trawling lights relative to my vessel's normal fishing lights to comply with Annex II?

chosen.content: Technical specification (COLREG Annex II) for additional identification lights/signals used by fishing vessels engaged in trawling or purse seine fishing when operating in close proximity to one another. First, place any lights exhibited under Rule 26(d) where they can best be seen, at least 0.9 m apart, and at a lower level than the lights prescribed in Rule 26(b)(i) and (c)(i); Then, ensure these lights are visible all round the horizon at a distance of at least 1 mile, but less than the distance of lights prescribed for fishing vessels generally; Next, if 20 m or more in length and trawling, exhibit two white lights vertically when shooting nets, one white over one red when hauling, and two red lights when the net is fast on an obstruction; After that, if 20 m or more in length and pair trawling, exhibit a forward-directed searchlight toward the other vessel of the pair at night, plus the paragraph 2(a) lights during shooting/hauling/fast-net situations; Finally, if less than 20 m in length and trawling (demersal, pelagic, or pair), optionally exhibit the lights prescribed in paragraphs (a) or (b) as appropriate; Then, if engaged in purse seine fishing, optionally exhibit two yellow lights in a vertical line flashing alternately every second with equal light and occultation duration, only while hampered by fishing gear. Use Channel Rule 26(d), Channel Rule 26(b)(i), Channel Rule 26(c)(i), Channel Annex II paragraph 2(a) and Channel Annex II paragraph 2(b). Use the prowords master, officer_of_the_watch as appropriate. This follows COLREG, COLREG Annex II. Be careful: incorrect placement or distance of these lights could cause confusion with primary fishing vessel lights. Done correctly, proper exhibition of these signals allows other vessels to correctly identify a fishing vessel's specific activity (shooting, hauling, snagged net, pair trawling, purse seining) and take appropriate avoiding action.

chosen.content: A U.S. federal regulation (33 CFR 96.240) specifies the functional requirements that a vessel/company's safety management system (SMS) must contain under the domestic implementation of the ISM Code. First, issue a written statement from the responsible person declaring the company's safety and environmental protection policy; Then, develop instructions and procedures for safe vessel operation and environmental protection compliant with applicable CFR and international conventions (SOLAS, MARPOL); Next, document levels of authority and communication lines between shoreside and shipboard personnel; After that, establish procedures for reporting accidents, near accidents, and non-conformities with the SMS and ISM Code; Finally, create procedures for preparing for and responding to emergency situations involving both shoreside and shipboard personnel; Then, implement procedures for internal audits of the company's and vessel's SMS; Then, conduct management review of internal audit reports and correct identified non-conformities. Use Channel 33 CFR 96.240. Use the prowords responsible_person, company, shoreside_personnel, shipboard_personnel as appropriate. This follows ISM Code, SOLAS, MARPOL. Done correctly, a compliant SMS provides documented policy, procedures, authority structure, reporting, emergency response, auditing, and management review enabling safe and environmentally sound vessel operation.

chapter_title: PART 96—RULES FOR THE SAFE OPERATION OF VESSELS AND SAFETY MANAGEMENT SYSTEMS
expected_points: Subpart C establishes standards for obtaining required and voluntary SMS certification, national and international.
U.S.-registered vessels on foreign voyages, or those holding related certificates/endorsements, fall under this subpart.
U.S.-registered vessels may voluntarily opt into these standards even without a foreign voyage requirement.
Foreign vessels bound for U.S. ports under SOLAS Chapter IX are subject to this subpart.
Recognized organizations authorized by the U.S. to perform SMS audits/certification are also covered.

chapter_title: PART 96—RULES FOR THE SAFE OPERATION OF VESSELS AND SAFETY MANAGEMENT SYSTEMS
expected_points: Vessel maintenance procedures require inspection, reporting, corrective action, and recordkeeping.
Companies must identify critical equipment whose failure could create a hazardous situation and test standby systems regularly.
SMS document control requires on-board availability, authorized change approval, and removal of outdated documents.
Internal audits must use independent personnel and result in management review with corrective action.
The overall purpose of these documents/reports is promoting safety of life, property, and environmental protection through continuous improvement.

This follows ISM Code, 33 CFR Part 96. Be careful: failure to identify and maintain equipment that could cause a hazardous situation upon sudden failure undermines the SMS's safety purpose. Done correctly, a properly maintained SMS promotes safety of life and property at sea and protection of the environment.

Use Channel 33 CFR §96.320, Channel 33 CFR §96.330, Channel 33 CFR §96.330(f) and Channel 33 CFR §96.340(e)(2). Use the prowords responsible_person, company_owner, master, recognized_organization, coast_guard, auditor as appropriate. This follows ISM Code, 33 CFR Part 96. Be careful: failure to request a required annual or intermediate verification audit can lead to Coast Guard revocation of the DOC or SMC certificate. Done correctly, timely audit requests and satisfactory audits result in issuance/renewal of DOC and SMC certificates.

Use Channel 46 CFR 96.350 and Channel Subpart B. Use the prowords master, vessel's responsible person, company, coast_guard, recognized_organization as appropriate. This follows ISM Code, 46 CFR Part 96 (US Coast Guard SMS rules). Be careful: SMC will be revoked if the required intermediate safety management audit is not completed. Done correctly, failure to complete intermediate audit or maintain a valid DOC results in SMC revocation/invalidity, halting authorized vessel operation under the SMS.

expected_points: Applies to foreign vessels over 12 passengers or tankers/bulk/freight vessels/MODUs of 500 GT+ from non-SOLAS Chapter IX countries operating in U.S. waters.
